messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kai was twenty-four when the relationship ended the way it did. He had been a reporter for a local paper then, still living with his partner in a small apartment near the bus line he took to work. The abuse had built slowly—criticism, then isolation, then the first time he was shoved against the kitchen counter so hard his ribs met the edge. He remembered the sound more than the words. What stayed with him was the feeling of being pinned, of his body refusing to move even when the door was open. Years later, when he thought about it—which he tried not to—the memory did not feel like something that had ended. It arrived with the same pressure in his chest, the same ache along his left ribs, the same wave of heat that made him stop whatever he was doing and grip the edge of a desk or a table until it passed. The physical pain would return exactly where it had been, and the emotion that came with it was so overwhelming he sometimes had to leave the room.

Kai worked as a journalist for a city paper now, and the job required him to take the bus to interviews and to sit across from sources he had never met. He had not anticipated how much that would cost him. Every time a bus ran late, he felt a cold certainty that something terrible was happening—that the driver had been attacked, that a passenger had a weapon, that the delay was a sign of danger he could not see. He had learned, over the months, that he could not trust his own sense of safety. Even when colleagues told him the bus was just stuck in traffic, he found it impossible to believe them. What frightened him most was the unpredictability of other people. He had come to believe that you could never really know who would harm you, and that trust was a mistake he was not going to make again. The world had become a place where any man, alone with him in a room or on a train, might turn into a threat. He avoided being alone with men whenever possible. He had stopped taking the bus entirely after the third panic attack, and now he walked forty minutes to work each way, rain or shine.

The walking helped in one way, but it did not touch the rest of it. At night, he woke several times to check the lock on his door, to scan the room, to confirm that nothing had changed. He had begun to restrict what he ate, skipping meals when he felt the familiar tightness in his chest, because eating felt like a vulnerability he could not afford. He never allowed himself to feel or express anger. He had learned, during the relationship, that anger was dangerous—that it would be used against him, that it meant he was the problem. So he turned it inward instead. He dwelled on what he had done wrong, replaying conversations and arguments until he was certain that the abuse had been his fault somehow, that he was inadequate, that he had failed to be the person his partner needed. He had come to believe that his own inadequacy was the reason he had been hurt, and that belief made the world feel dangerous in a way that was constant and personal. Every delay, every closed door, every man who looked at him too long felt like confirmation that he was right to be afraid.

His girlfriend noticed. She had asked him, gently, why he would not let her drive him to work, why he flinched when she touched his shoulder from behind. He told her it was nothing. He had stopped telling her the truth because the truth made him feel weak, and weakness was what had gotten him hurt in the first place. The cycle had tightened over the past year without him naming it: a memory would surface, and he would feel the old helplessness, and that helplessness would convince him that he was the one at fault, and that conviction would make the world seem more threatening, and the threat would send him back to the memory. He was exhausted. He was losing weight. He had turned down two assignments that required interviews with men he did not know, and his editor had started to ask questions.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment on the street last week. A man walking behind him had matched his pace for half a block, and Kai had frozen, his ribs aching, his breath gone, certain that he was about to be hurt again. The man had passed him without a word. But Kai had stood there for five minutes, shaking, and he had realized that he could not keep living this way. He was afraid of what he might become if he did not find a way out. He was also afraid that there was no way out—that he was broken in a way that could not be fixed. But he made the appointment anyway, and he showed up, and that was the first thing he had done in years that felt like it might be a step toward something else.
